sourceBindings.text: A rotation is a planned sequence of crops on the same land. You will justify each year from field evidence, draw arrows that follow the year numbers, and test whether the plan works for the farm's nutrients, pests, season, water, equipment and market.
Draw a three-year crop sequence with arrows that match the numbered years and justify each year using nutrients, host pests, roots and residues rather than crop names alone.
Explain at least three potential rotation benefits with examples and limits, including why neither universal rootworm control nor a complete nitrogen refund is guaranteed.
Defend a different or four-year plan using site and crop evidence, land occupancy, market, equipment and water constraints; allow a valid alternative to the model sequence.

sourceBindings.text: Arrange maize, soybean and wheat under Years 1, 2 and 3. Draw two forward arrows, 1→2 and 2→3, and one return arrow, 3→1: three directed links in total. Justify every transition.
For nutrient, pest and soil-cover/root benefits, write one plausible mechanism, one crop example and one condition that could limit it.
Using the exact 10-ha temperate case and your prior eight-crop shortlist, complete a three-year crop/reason table. Compare it with the model and one peer plan, then revise your own justification.
Optionally extend to Year 4 using a cover crop or another crop. State its season, duration, termination or harvest, market/equipment implications and water need.
Compare every arrow with the printed year number; reversed direction or a guaranteed nitrogen claim triggers revision.

The trainer facilitates the 15-minute planning and 10-minute discussion portions of the 45-minute case. Each learner submits an individual plan and reasoned revision. This knowledge step does not certify a physical field skill.

sourceBindings.text: crop rotation
A planned sequence of crops on the same area of land across seasons or years.
host crop
A crop on which a particular pest can survive or reproduce; host status is pest-specific.
nitrogen credit
An evidence-based estimate of nitrogen supplied to a later crop by a prior crop or its residues, not a guaranteed amount from a crop name.
crop residue
Plant material remaining after harvest, whose return or removal changes soil cover and nutrient/carbon flows.
cover crop
A crop grown mainly to cover and manage soil; its benefit depends on species, season and management.
monocropping
Repeated production of the same crop on the same field over successive seasons or years.
